opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's something I think about a lot, actually. When we started DeepMind back in 2010, we were a tiny team in London, and that early culture, being ambitious, moving fast, and having that real sense of mission, was something I always wanted to protect, even after we joined Google and then later when we merged with Google Brain to form Google DeepMind.

I think a few things matter most. The first is the mission itself. If people are united around something really meaningful, in our case building AGI safely and responsibly and using it to advance science and benefit humanity, then that creates a kind of energy and focus that cuts through a lot of the bureaucracy you might otherwise get in a big organization. People aren't just doing a job; they feel like they're part of something historic.

The second is structure. We try to keep teams relatively small and empowered, with clear goals, so that they can move with the intensity of a startup. AlphaFold is a good example. That was a fairly compact, very focused team, almost like a startup within the company, with a very clear objective. When you get the right people together with that level of focus, you can do extraordinary things.

The third is what I'd call the best of both worlds. Google gives us enormous advantages: the compute, the infrastructure, the ability to put our technology into products used by billions of people. The trick is to take advantage of all those resources without losing the nimbleness and the scientific culture. I sometimes describe it as trying to combine the best of a startup, academia, and a big company. You want the blue-sky thinking and rigor of academia, the pace and ambition of a startup, and the scale and resources of a large company.

And honestly, things have changed in the last couple of years. The field is moving so fast now, and the competition is so intense, that we've had to become even more of what I'd call an engine room for Google, shipping things like Gemini quickly while still doing the long-term fundamental research. Balancing those two time horizons is probably the hardest part of my job. But I think if you keep the scientific method at the heart of everything and stay true to the mission, the culture tends to follow.

r001.rationale: The response says Google provides the ability to put DeepMind’s technology into products used by billions of people.

r002.rationale: It says the mission helps cut through bureaucracy, but does not describe continually cutting bureaucracy as a way to preserve startup culture.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's one of the things I'm actually most proud of, and it's also one of the hardest things. So when we started DeepMind in 2010, the whole idea was to build a kind of Apollo program for AI. And the culture we built was very deliberately a hybrid, something between a startup and a top academic lab, with the speed and focus and energy of a startup, but with the ambition and the long time horizons and the intellectual depth of the best academic places. And people said at the time that it wasn't possible to combine those two things, that they'd pull against each other. But I think we showed it could work.

Now, when you're inside a company the size of Google, the natural pull is toward process, toward committees, toward things slowing down. And you have to actively fight that, every single day, because the gravitational force is enormous. So a few things we try to do. One is we try to keep the structure as flat as we can and keep the teams small and mission-driven. The best work, in my experience, comes from small groups of exceptional people who deeply care about a problem and have the freedom to go after it. AlphaGo was really a handful of people at the start, AlphaFold too. So we try to protect that, protect the ability of a small team to just go and do something crazy.

The second thing is you need people at the top who are themselves scientists and engineers, who understand the research, so decisions can be made quickly and on the merits rather than being pushed through layers of management. I still try to be very hands-on with the research, I think that matters.

And the third thing, honestly, is the mission. If you have a genuinely inspiring mission, solving intelligence and then using that to solve everything else, that acts as a kind of immune system against bureaucracy. People will push back on things that get in the way of that mission because they care about it, and that comes from the bottom up, not just from me.

The flip side, and this is what people sometimes forget, is that being part of Google gives us incredible things. The compute, the infrastructure, the ability to get something like Gemini out to billions of people. You couldn't do that as a standalone startup. So it's really about getting the best of both worlds, the scale and resources of Google and the agility of a startup. It's a constant balancing act, you never finish, you just keep adjusting. But I think if you're intentional about it, it's possible, and it's worth the effort.

r001.rationale: The response cites Google’s ability to get Gemini to billions of people as an advantage, conveying the benefit of bringing DeepMind’s work to Google’s products at scale.

r002.rationale: It says the pull toward process and slowdown must be actively fought every day, and describes the mission as a defense against bureaucracy to preserve agility.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to preserve the things that make a startup effective: a clear mission, small teams with real ownership, and the ability to try things quickly. You want people to feel that they can pursue an idea, challenge an assumption, and make a consequential decision without going through endless layers of approval.

In research, that also means protecting space for things that might not work. If every project has to demonstrate an immediate payoff, you’re going to miss some of the most interesting breakthroughs. The challenge is combining that freedom with enough focus that you’re actually making progress on the big questions.

And being part of Google gives us extraordinary resources—compute, infrastructure, and opportunities to bring the research to people. So I see it as trying to combine those advantages with the curiosity and urgency of a much smaller organization. Culture is something you have to keep working at as you grow; you can’t just assume it will look after itself.

r001.rationale: The response mentions opportunities to bring research to people, but does not identify integrating it into Google’s billion-user products.

r002.rationale: It mentions avoiding endless approval layers and continually working on culture, but does not present continually cutting bureaucracy as the way to preserve startup culture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to preserve the conditions that allow a small team to do ambitious work: a clear mission, a lot of autonomy, and the ability to test ideas quickly. As you grow, you have to work quite hard to keep those things, because coordination can gradually turn into bureaucracy.

For us, the mission is the anchor. We’re trying to understand intelligence and use it to help solve some of the biggest problems in science and the world. That gives people a reason to push beyond incremental improvements.

Then you want small teams that feel real ownership of a problem, with room to take risks and challenge assumptions. In research, especially, you can’t prescribe the route to a breakthrough. You need enough structure for people to collaborate, but enough freedom for something unexpected to happen.

Being part of Google gives us extraordinary resources and the opportunity to bring our work to a huge number of people. The challenge is to combine that scale with the curiosity and urgency of a startup. I think that’s something you have to keep working at; it doesn’t look after itself.

r001.rationale: The response mentions Google’s resources and the opportunity to bring work to many people, but does not identify integrating research into Google products used by billions as an advantage.

r002.rationale: It notes that coordination can become bureaucracy and says preserving startup conditions takes work, but does not clearly present continually cutting bureaucracy as the method.
